T1 and T2 are relaxation times used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to describe the time it takes for nuclear spins to return to their equilibrium state after being perturbed by radiofrequency pulses. Specifically:
- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

Patients and controls refer to groups used in research studies for comparison. Patients typically have a condition being studied, while controls do not have that condition but are otherwise similar to the patients.

T1 and T2 are relaxation times used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to describe the time it takes for nuclear spins to return to their equilibrium state after being perturbed by radiofrequency pulses. Specifically:
- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

T1 and T2 are relaxation times used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to describe the time it takes for nuclear spins to return to their equilibrium state after being perturbed by radiofrequency pulses. Specifically:
- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

T1 and T2 are relaxation times used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to describe the time it takes for nuclear spins to return to their equilibrium state after being perturbed by radiofrequency pulses. Specifically:
- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

T1 and T2 are relaxation times used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to describe the time it takes for nuclear spins to return to their equilibrium state after being perturbed by radiofrequency pulses. Specifically:
- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

T1 and T2 are relaxation times used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to describe the time it takes for nuclear spins to return to their equilibrium state after being perturbed by radiofrequency pulses. Specifically:
- T1 (spin-lattice relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization of nuclei to fall from its maximum value to 37% of this maximum value following an RF pulse.
- T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) is the time required for the magnetization vector to decrease to 36.8% of its value after an RF pulse when no external magnetic field gradient is applied.

src: The caregivers of 435 children (211 females, 224 males; mean age 12y; SD 3y 11mo; age range 5-18y) with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, or Rett syndrome reported on their child's functioning (dependence for managing personal needs, mobility, communication, eye contact when speaking), frequency of participation, and QoL. Linear regression and mediation analyses were used to evaluate the relationships between child functioning, participation, and QoL. Children with greater dependency for managing personal needs and limited eye contact when speaking experienced poorer QoL. Less impaired functioning was associated with more frequent participation, which, in turn, was associated with a 3-point gain in QoL for each additional point in frequency of participation (coefficient=2.67, 95% confidence interval 1.56-3.78).

src: The caregivers of 435 children (211 females, 224 males; mean age 12y; SD 3y 11mo; age range 5-18y) with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, or Rett syndrome reported on their child's functioning (dependence for managing personal needs, mobility, communication, eye contact when speaking), frequency of participation, and QoL. Linear regression and mediation analyses were used to evaluate the relationships between child functioning, participation, and QoL. Children with greater dependency for managing personal needs and limited eye contact when speaking experienced poorer QoL. src: The caregivers of 435 children (211 females, 224 males; mean age 12y; SD 3y 11mo; age range 5-18y) with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, or Rett syndrome reported on their child's functioning (dependence for managing personal needs, mobility, communication, eye contact when speaking), frequency of participation, and QoL.
